title: Recombinant DNA Technology and Molecular Testing — DOMiNANCE Originals
source: KNUST Recombinant DNA Technology lecture and Nucleic Acid Metabolism lectures

questions.stem: What is a restriction endonuclease primarily used for in recombinant DNA construction?

options.label: A
options.text: Translating RNA into amino acid chains

options.label: D
options.text: Joining amino acids by peptide bonds

questions.why: Restriction enzymes recognize specific DNA sequences and cut at or near those sites.

questions.stem: Why can bacteria protect their own DNA from certain endogenous restriction enzymes?

options.label: C
options.text: Their DNA lacks all recognition sequences

questions.why: Restriction-modification systems methylate host recognition sites to protect them from cleavage.

questions.stem: Which enzyme covalently joins a gene insert to the DNA backbone of a cut plasmid?
questions.why: DNA ligase seals compatible DNA ends by making phosphodiester bonds.

questions.stem: Which plasmid feature permits autonomous replication after introduction into bacteria?
questions.why: An origin of replication permits the vector to duplicate inside the host.

questions.stem: What is a selectable marker in an expression plasmid commonly used to do?

options.label: C
options.text: Change the genetic code of host cells

questions.why: Antibiotic-resistance markers allow growth of transformed cells under selection.

questions.stem: Which method directly introduces plasmid DNA into bacterial cells by short electrical pulses?
questions.why: Electroporation transiently permeabilizes cell membranes to facilitate DNA entry.

questions.stem: Which vector combines features of plasmids and bacteriophage lambda to accommodate relatively large inserts?
questions.why: Cosmids carry lambda cos sites along with plasmid features and can accommodate larger inserts than common plasmids.

questions.stem: Which vector is designed to carry very large cloned DNA fragments in a bacterial host?
questions.why: BACs can maintain large genomic inserts in bacteria.

questions.stem: What distinguishes a shuttle vector from a vector limited to one host species?

options.label: E
options.text: A requirement for only RNA inserts

questions.why: Shuttle vectors carry functions that allow maintenance in two different organisms, such as bacteria and yeast.

questions.stem: Why is complementary DNA often preferred for expressing human insulin in bacteria?

options.label: C
options.text: It is made only from proteins

questions.why: cDNA is made from mature mRNA and therefore lacks introns that bacteria cannot splice in the same way.

questions.stem: Which enzyme converts a mature messenger RNA template into complementary DNA?
questions.why: Reverse transcriptase makes a DNA strand using RNA as its template.

questions.stem: What is a major difference between a genomic DNA library and a cDNA library?

options.label: A
options.text: Genomic libraries contain only translated exons

options.label: B
options.text: cDNA libraries contain all chromosomal promoters

options.label: C
options.text: cDNA libraries contain all telomeric repeats

options.label: D
options.text: Genomic libraries preserve introns and flanks

options.label: E
options.text: Both libraries are limited to plasmid RNA only

questions.why: A genomic library samples whole genomic DNA; a cDNA library represents transcribed RNA-derived sequences.

questions.stem: Which property makes a cDNA library dependent on the tissue and condition sampled?

options.label: B
options.text: It contains all loci at equal abundance

options.label: C
options.text: It requires loss of the ribosomal code

questions.why: cDNA synthesis uses the mRNA pool present in the sampled tissue, so unexpressed genes are poorly represented.

questions.stem: Which component defines the two ends of a DNA region amplified in conventional PCR?
questions.why: Forward and reverse primers anneal to opposite strands flanking the target.

questions.stem: Which enzyme property is essential for standard repeated high-temperature PCR cycling?
questions.why: Thermostable DNA polymerase withstands repeated denaturation steps.

questions.stem: What is the principal purpose of the high-temperature first step in each PCR cycle?

options.label: B
options.text: Separate the two DNA template strands

questions.why: Denaturation at about 95°C produces single-stranded DNA for subsequent primer binding.

questions.stem: What occurs during the annealing phase of a conventional PCR cycle?

options.label: A
options.text: DNA polymerase adds all amino acids

options.label: C
options.text: Taq polymerase removes all target DNA

options.label: E
options.text: DNA ligase repairs every chromosomal break

questions.why: Reduced temperature permits primers to base-pair with their matching target sites.

questions.stem: Why is the extension phase of standard Taq PCR often performed near 72 degrees Celsius?

options.label: A
options.text: It supports DNA extension by Taq polymerase

options.label: B
options.text: It completely denatures the PCR template

options.label: C
options.text: It prevents every primer from binding

options.label: E
options.text: It allows ribosomes to synthesize Taq protein

questions.why: Taq polymerase extends annealed primers most efficiently near its optimal working temperature.

questions.stem: Under ideal conditions, what is the approximate amplification factor after ten PCR cycles from one double-stranded target?
questions.why: Ideal exponential PCR roughly doubles target DNA each cycle, giving 2^10 after ten cycles.

questions.stem: Why is conventional PCR poorly suited to amplifying DNA with completely unknown flanking sequences?

options.label: D
options.text: RNA ligase must first join each base

questions.why: Primer design normally requires knowledge of the sequences bordering the region to be amplified.

questions.stem: Which product is directly amplified in standard reverse-transcription PCR?
questions.why: Reverse transcriptase first converts RNA to cDNA, which is then amplified by DNA PCR.

questions.stem: What primarily determines DNA-fragment migration through an agarose gel under an electric field?
questions.why: Smaller DNA fragments generally migrate farther through a gel under comparable conditions.

questions.stem: Which technique identifies a specific DNA fragment after electrophoresis and probe hybridization?
questions.why: Southern blotting transfers and detects DNA using labelled nucleic-acid probes.

questions.stem: Which laboratory blotting technique is most appropriate for detecting a specific RNA transcript?
questions.why: Northern blots detect RNA, whereas Southern blots detect DNA and Western blots detect proteins.

questions.stem: What can a restriction fragment length polymorphism reveal in a genetic test?

options.label: A
options.text: A change only in antibody Fc sequence

options.label: B
options.text: A change in peptide charge without DNA

options.label: C
options.text: A change in serum albumin concentration

options.label: D
options.text: A change only in mitochondrial membrane

options.label: E
options.text: A change in DNA restriction-site pattern

questions.why: Sequence variants can alter restriction sites and hence the sizes of DNA fragments after digestion.

questions.stem: Which highly variable DNA markers are often compared for forensic profiling and paternity testing?
questions.why: STR alleles differ in repeat number between individuals, providing informative genetic markers.

questions.stem: How can DNA typing most decisively exclude a proposed biological father at an informative locus?

options.label: A
options.text: Child shares a paternal allele at every locus

options.label: B
options.text: Father and child share one STR allele

options.label: C
options.text: The mother carries both child alleles

options.label: D
options.text: Child has an allele absent from both parents

options.label: E
options.text: The child carries one maternal allele

questions.why: An offspring allele not explained by either tested biological parent indicates nonpaternity or an atypical event requiring verification.

questions.stem: Which application is a common use of gene-specific DNA probes in inherited disease testing?
questions.why: Molecular probes and allele-specific methods detect particular DNA variants associated with genetic disorders.

questions.stem: What distinguishes somatic gene therapy from germline genetic modification?

options.label: A
options.text: Somatic modifications alter every future gamete

options.label: B
options.text: Germline changes affect only skin cells

options.label: C
options.text: Somatic changes are not intended to be inherited

options.label: D
options.text: Somatic modifications never affect protein synthesis

options.label: E
options.text: Somatic treatment does not involve DNA

questions.why: Somatic gene therapy targets body cells; germline editing can be transmitted to offspring.

questions.stem: Which component of CRISPR-Cas gene editing most directly specifies the target sequence?
questions.why: A guide RNA directs a Cas nuclease to a complementary genomic region alongside a required PAM.

questions.stem: Which technique can rapidly produce many copies of one known DNA segment without cloning it in bacteria?
questions.why: PCR amplifies selected target DNA exponentially using primers, dNTPs, and a thermostable polymerase.

questions.stem: Why can a restriction site mutation be detected by comparing digested DNA fragment patterns?

options.label: A
options.text: Restriction enzymes read RNA codons only

options.label: B
options.text: Gel electrophoresis separates by antibody class

options.label: D
options.text: Different cut sites produce different lengths

options.label: E
options.text: DNA bases always bind the same probe

questions.why: A mutation creating or eliminating a restriction site changes the sizes of fragments released on digestion.
